query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In the solidified, Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy, the dynamic mechanical response is governed by a temperature- and strain rate–dependent shift in the active deformation mechanism. Specifically, under moderate conditions, dislocation glide dominates; however, as strain rate increases (or temperature decreases), a transition occurs in which an effective reduction in stacking fault energy promotes deformation twinning and/or a phase transformation (e.g., a FCC to BCC change) that assists in maintaining the strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneous, cast or homogenized Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy with controlled and uniform grain size and minimal preexisting defects.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or compression tests) across a spectrum of strain rates and temperatures.
generation.conditions: Testing under varying temperatures (from cryogenic to elevated) and a range of strain rates (from quasi-static to dynamic/shock conditions) to capture the full regime of deformation mechanisms.
generation.structural_mediator: Microstructural features such as grain boundaries, twin boundaries, and regions of locally altered stacking fault energy that mediate the balance between dislocation movement and deformation twinning/phase transformation.
generation.mechanism: Temperature and strain-rate variations modulate the effective stacking fault energy in the Co‐free alloy, controlling the competition between dislocation glide and mechanisms such as deformation twinning or phase transformation. At lower temperatures or higher strain rates, the decreased mobility of dislocations (possibly due to a lower effective stacking fault energy) leads to an increased role of twinning or phase transformation, which helps maintain ductility while bolstering strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable transition in the deformation mechanism: at moderate conditions, stress–strain responses will reflect dislocation glide with steady hardening; under high strain rate or low temperature, an increase in work hardening rate, enhanced strength without a loss in ductility, and microstructural evidence (e.g., increased twin boundaries or phase variants) consistent with a shift in active deformation mechanism.
generation.baseline: The behavior observed under moderate strain rate and ambient temperature conditions where dislocation glide predominates and no significant twinning or phase transformation is evident.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected to hold for the Co‐free, equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy and may not apply if dramatic microstructural changes occur (e.g., due to extreme grain refinement or secondary phase precipitation) or for alloys with significantly different compositions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise strain rate and temperature thresholds for the transition between dislocation-dominated and twinning/phase transformation mechanisms are currently uncertain and require systematic experimental mapping.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare homogeneous FeNiCrMn samples with uniform grain sizes. Subject samples to uniaxial tensile or compression tests across a matrix of temperatures (e.g., cryogenic, room, elevated) and strain rates (from quasi-static to high, dynamic rates). Employ in situ characterization techniques such as electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), high-speed digital image correlation (DIC), or transmission electron microscopy (TEM) post-mortem, to identify the dominant deformation mechanisms (dislocation slip vs. twinning or phase transformation) under each test condition.
measurements: Stress–strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility, and work hardening rates)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., detection of twin boundaries, new phase formation, and dislocation densities)
Dynamic observations (e.g., in situ DIC to capture transient strain localization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the systematic variation of strain rate and temperature does not result in a corresponding shift from dislocation glide to enhanced twinning or phase transformation—as evidenced by the absence of microstructural changes, work hardening rate alterations, or changes in ductility—then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

The HEA exhibits exceptional properties, including a superior yield strength of approximately 1.8 GPa and a high hardness of around 454 Hv. These exceptional properties make it suitable for use in shock environments. Computational studies have reported an FCC–BCC phase transformation phenomenon in this HEA under tension loading, indicating that this phase transition can enhance ductility while retaining high strength []. The phase transformation is highly dependent on crystalline orientation and strain rate. Furthermore, Wang et al. While the yield strength and KJIc fracture toughness of the medium-entropy CrCoNi and high-entropy CrMnFeCoNi alloys are comparable, the tensile strengths, tensile ductility and work of fracture of the CrCoNi alloy are significantly higher, by respectively ∼15, ∼30 and ∼50%, at room temperature. At cryogenic temperatures, the strengths of the two alloys are comparable (σUTS∼1,300 MPa at 77 K), but the KJIc fracture toughness, tensile ductility and work of fracture are again markedly higher in the CrCoNi alloy, by ∼25, ∼27 and ∼31%, respectively. The yield strength, σy, at 77 K is slightly below that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, which we believe is due to the non-uniform grain size of our present material (Fig. 1b–d). Consistent with this notion, in a previous study where the grain size of CrCoNi was uniform and comparable to that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, the tensile properties of the three-component alloy were found to exceed those of the five-component alloy at all temperatures.

Unlike conventional metallic alloys, which are comprised of a base (solvent) and alloying (solute) elements, high entropy alloys (HEAs) are a class of structural alloys first introduced by Cantor et al. and Yeh et al. that consist of multiple principal elements in equiatomic or near equiatomic concentrations. Owing to their multi-principal element compositions, HEAs are characterized by unique combinations of properties, including mechanical strength,,, hardness,, and wear, and corrosion resistance. The use of multiple principal elements in far-from dilute concentrations unlocks infinite possibilities of combinations of properties and functionalities that are not typically found in conventional metallic alloys. Numerous recent studies on 3d transition metal HEAs, such as CoCrFeMnNi,, CoCrFeNi,, CoFeMnNi, CoCrMnNi, and Co0.25Cr0.1Fe2Mn1.35Ni1.3, have explored the impact of temperature,, grain size, alloy composition, strain rate, strain levels, and phase transformations, on the mechanical behavior of these alloys. The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, or so-called Cantor, alloy is a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase alloy that has been regarded as a model system to many single-phase HEAs.
